title: First-Degree AV Block — "If the R is Far From P, It's a First Degree"

sections.overview: Recognize first-degree AV block: a prolonged but constant PR interval (> 0.20 sec) with every P wave still followed by a QRS — the impulse is slow but always gets through.
sections.keyTerms:
- **R** — R wave (QRS complex)
- **P** — P wave
- **Far** — Prolonged PR interval
sections.collegeNotes:
Recognize first-degree AV block: a prolonged but constant PR interval (> 0.20 sec) with every P wave still followed by a QRS — the impulse is slow but always gets through.

### R — R wave (QRS complex)

The ventricle's beat — "the wife" in the husband/wife analogy

The QRS complex reflects ventricular depolarization. In first-degree AV block a QRS follows every P wave — no beats are dropped. Its width depends on where the delay is; with a delay confined to the AV node the QRS is usually narrow.

**Physiology.** A QRS appears every time the depolarization wave successfully reaches the ventricles. In first-degree block conduction is delayed (not blocked), so the QRS always follows — just later.

**Safety.** Confirm on the monitor that every P wave is followed by a QRS; the relationship must be constant. If QRS complexes start dropping, the rhythm has progressed to a higher-degree block.

### P — P wave

The atrium's beat — "the husband" firing from the SA node

The P wave reflects atrial depolarization originating in the SA node. In first-degree AV block the SA node and atria are normal; the problem is entirely downstream at the AV node, where the impulse is delayed before reaching the ventricles.

**Physiology.** The SA node is the heart's natural pacemaker (60–100 bpm). In first-degree block it keeps firing normally and the atria respond normally — the rhythm's only abnormality is the delay between P and QRS.

**Safety.** A normal, regular P wave with a prolonged PR tells you the atria are fine — look downstream (AV node, medications, ischemia) for the cause of the delay.

### Far — Prolonged PR interval

A consistent but stretched-out delay between the P wave and the R wave

The PR interval (normal 0.12–0.20 sec, or 3–5 small boxes) is the time from the start of atrial depolarization to the start of ventricular depolarization — essentially AV conduction time. In first-degree block the PR interval is constantly greater than 0.20 sec but fixed.

**Physiology.** The AV node normally delays the impulse ~0.1 sec so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract. In first-degree block that delay is pathologically lengthened (disease, vagal tone, or drugs), but conduction still completes on every beat.

**Safety.** First-degree block is usually benign by itself, but a new, sudden PR prolongation can be the first sign of digoxin/beta-blocker/calcium-channel-blocker toxicity or ischemia — investigate the cause rather than dismissing it.

sections.eli10:
It's the mildest traffic jam in the heart's electrical road. The signal from the top rooms to the bottom rooms is slow, but every signal still gets through — nothing is blocked, just delayed.

**R — R wave (QRS complex).** The "R" is the tall spike on the ECG that shows the bottom rooms (ventricles) squeezing. In the story, the R wave is the wife who does the heavy lifting of pumping blood out. In first-degree block she always shows up for work — just a little late, every single time.

**P — P wave.** The "P" is the little bump before the spike that shows the top rooms (atria) squeezing. It is the husband in the story. In first-degree block the husband always calls home — the SA node fires normally and the atria contract on time, every time.

**Far — Prolonged PR interval.** "Far" means the husband and wife stand a little farther apart than usual — the time between the P bump and the R spike is stretched out. The distance is always the same stretched length, and they always still connect.

- Far = Prolonged PR interval — A consistent but stretched-out delay between the P wave and the R wave
